newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Strike hits hard in S.Africa's Eastern Cape.
newsitem.headline: Strike hits hard in S.Africa's Eastern Cape.

text.p: South Africa's largest trade union federation started a week of protests on Monday against new employment laws.

The 1.9-million member Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) chose the Eastern Cape province to start four days of 24-hour regional strikes, hitting hard at the economically depressed area which is home of the country's vehicle industry.

The Congress wants six months' maternity leave for workers, four of them with pay, and a 40-hour working week to be phased in over five years. Planned legislation promises only a 46-hour week and shorter maternity leave.

Regional Chamber of Commerce chief Kevin Wakeford estimated lost turnover at 117 million rand ($25 million) and said around 70 percent of workers went on strike in the greater Port Elizabeth-Uitenhage area.

The strike hit automobile manufacturing and ancillary sectors, including engineering, textiles and tyres, he said. Buses and taxis did not run in the metropolitan region -- the economic hub of the province. Marches on business institutions passed off peacefully.
Wakeford estimated lost wages at around 23.6 million rand, and a loss of 60 million rand in the area's contribution to gross domestic product.
He said the Eastern Cape's fragile economy could not sustain continuing mass action.

"The time has arrived for the labour movement to get real and accept that we are now an inextricable part of the international economy which is highly competitive and unsentimental to domestic problems," he added.
Cosatu has organised the four days of action to back up its demands over proposed changes to the labour laws enshrined in the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill. It says there will be no compromise.
Business has agreed to reduce the working week by an hour to 45 hours, but refuses to commit itself to a 40-hour week.
Employers' groups have argued that some of the bill's provisions could raise employment costs, already higher than many competitors', deterring job creation.
Umbrella group Business South Africa negotiator Adrian du Plessis called for a resumption of negotiations and said the strike would not help to end the impasse over the proposed law.
Cosatu spokeswoman Nowetu Mpati told Reuters there was no reason to resume already-prolonged talks with business, since no new proposals had been made.

Labour Minister Tito Mboweni has repeatedly said the employment bill cannot become law this year unless broad consensus is reached between business and labour, in time for its presentation to parliament on September 15.
He was unavailable for comment on Monday.
